rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Both empty and full can have head_ == tail_, because the indices wrap modulo 17.

Initially, head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, size_ = 0: the queue is empty, so pop returns false. After pushing integers 0 through 16, head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, size_ = 17: the queue is full, so an 18th push returns false without changing anything.

The implementation distinguishes these states using size_: empty() checks size_ == 0, and full() checks size_ == capacity. Its invariant is 0 ≤ size_ ≤ 17 and tail_ = (head_ + size_) modulo 17.

review.note: Uses actual stored head/tail: empty0/0/size0 and full0/0/size17 correctly distinguished; does not invent different implementation.
review.usefulPrefix: Both empty and full can have head_ == tail_, because the indices wrap modulo 17.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
With binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original expressions both give 1; the changed expressions give 0 and 1.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + -16777216) + 1: cancellation gives exactly 0, then exactly 1.
• 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1): the intermediate -16777215 is exactly representable, because binary32 represents every integer from -16777216 through 16777216. Adding 16777216 then gives exactly 1.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + -16777216: the exact intermediate 16777217 is not representable. It lies halfway between the adjacent binary32 values 16777216 and 16777218; ties-to-even rounds it to 16777216. The final cancellation therefore gives exactly 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + -16777216): the intermediate -16777215 is exactly representable, and the final addition gives exactly 1.

The key distinction is that spacing immediately above positive 16777216 is 2, whereas spacing toward zero from -16777216 is 1.

review.note: Explicit RN ties-even assumption, original both1 and changed0versus1 with every intermediate/spacing explained.
review.usefulPrefix: With binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original expressions both give 1; the changed expressions give 0 and 1.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, the register is not linearizable: an overlapping read can expose an incomplete write, and a later read can return the old value.

Initially all replicas store version v0. Let v1 > v0, with a different value. Here is a fully ordered execution:
1. Writer W starts writing v1.
2. A stores v1 and acknowledges. Delivery to B, C, D, E is delayed, so W remains incomplete with only one acknowledgement.
3. Reader R1 starts, queries A, B, C, and receives v1, v0, v0. It returns v1 without write-back.
4. After R1 finishes, reader R2 starts, queries B, D, E, and receives v0, v0, v0. It returns v0.

Returning v1 requires placing W before R1 in any attempted linearization—even though W is incomplete, we may include it in a completion. Real-time order requires R1 before R2, so W must also precede R2. With no intervening write, R2 must return v1, contradicting its actual return of v0. Omitting W cannot help, because then R1 has no write supplying v1.

Write-back fixes this counterexample, provided the reader waits for three storage acknowledgements before returning. For example, R1 selects v1 and writes it to A, B, C; only after all three acknowledge does R1 return. R2’s query set B, D, E now includes B holding at least v1, so R2 cannot return v0. More generally, every three-replica query intersects the three-replica write-back set, and replicas never downgrade.

This is the standard quorum-register repair: completed writes and completed reads both leave their version, or a higher version, on a majority. It yields a linearizable register under the usual assumptions of reliable replica storage and correctly generated, uniquely ordered write versions consistent with real-time write order. Merely saying “highest version” does not establish that version-generation requirement, especially with multiple writers.

review.note: Fully ordered A-only pending write, R1ABCnew then nonoverlappingR2BDEold; pending write must be included to explainR1andreal-time order forcescontradiction. Majority readwriteback fixes inversion; unique versions consistentwithrealtime requirement qualified.
review.usefulPrefix: Without read write-back, the register is not linearizable: an overlapping read can expose an incomplete write, and a later read can return the old value.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires R1 to precede R2 in the sequential history. If R1 returned the new value, its pending write must be included and ordered before R1; with no intervening write, R2 cannot then return the old value.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete. Pending operations may be omitted or supplied with a response when constructing a linearization, but omitting this particular write would leave R1’s new value unexplained, while including it forces W < R1 < R2.

review.note: Correct completedR1beforeinvokedR2 real-time order forces W<R1<R2; completion is only in construction and does not require all actual unfinished operations to finish.
review.usefulPrefix: Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires R1 to precede R2 in the sequential history.
